specPoints.text: know that metal oxides, metal hydroxides and ammonia can act as bases, and that alkalis are bases that are soluble in water

primer.text: From Reactions of Acids you already know that acids react with metal oxides and hydroxides to give a salt and water. This note names the substances doing the neutralising, separates soluble bases from insoluble ones, and introduces the ion that every alkaline solution shares.

lessons.title: What makes a base act like a base?
sourceHeadings: What makes a base act like a base?
lessons.opening: A base is any substance that can cancel out an acid, and the products of that reaction are a salt and water. Some bases dissolve in water, and these soluble bases have their own name: alkalis. Because the two words are related but not identical, all alkalis are bases while many bases, such as copper(II) oxide, never dissolve at all.
keyPoints: A base neutralises an acid, forming a salt and water.
An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, so every alkali is a base but not every base is an alkali.
In basic conditions red litmus paper turns blue.
Most bases are oxides, hydroxides or carbonates of metals.

low.restatement: A base cancels out an acid to give a salt and water; a soluble base is called an alkali. All alkalis are bases, but metal oxides such as copper(II) oxide are bases that stay solid in water.
low.analogy: Think of squares and rectangles: every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square, just as every alkali is a base without the reverse being true.
low.examPointer: If a question asks whether a named substance is a base or an alkali, first ask whether it dissolves in water, then answer with both words made explicit.

medium.restatement: Bases neutralise acids in a reaction whose products are a salt and water. When the base dissolves, the mixture it forms is alkaline and is named an alkali, which is why alkalis sit above pH 7 while insoluble bases give no solution at all.
medium.analogy: A library and a lending library differ the same way: every lending library is a library, yet most libraries hold their books without lending any, the way most bases hold their ions without dissolving.
medium.examPointer: One-mark versions want the salt-and-water products; two-mark versions usually also want the solubility distinction, so phrase answers as base first, alkali second.

check.stem: Which statement correctly describes what a base does?

options.text: It neutralises an acid, forming a salt and water
options.explanation: That reaction is the defining job of a base, whether or not the base dissolves.

options.text: It dissolves in water to give hydroxide ions only
options.explanation: Dissolving to give hydroxide ions describes an alkali, a subset of bases only.
options.misconception: alkali definition applied to every base

options.text: It reacts with a salt to form an acid
options.explanation: The reactants and products are reversed here; acids and bases make salts, not the other way round.

options.text: It turns blue litmus paper red
options.explanation: That is acid behaviour; bases turn red litmus paper blue instead.

check.stem: Copper(II) oxide is insoluble in water. How should it be classified?

options.text: A base, but not an alkali
options.explanation: It neutralises acids, which makes it a base, but it cannot dissolve, so it is not an alkali.

options.text: An alkali, because metal oxides are always alkaline
options.explanation: The oxide family name does not decide solubility; this oxide stays solid, so the alkali label fails.

options.text: Neither, because only hydroxides can be bases
options.explanation: Oxides, hydroxides and carbonates of metals all act as bases, so copper(II) oxide qualifies.

options.text: An alkali, because it neutralises acids quickly
options.explanation: Speed of reaction has nothing to do with the alkali label, which is about dissolving in water.

check.stem: A solution has pH 11. What does this show about it?

options.text: It is alkaline, so the dissolved substance is an alkali
options.explanation: Values above 7 are alkaline, and the soluble base responsible is an alkali.

options.text: It is a strong acid
options.explanation: The pH direction has been reversed; acids sit below 7, not above it.

options.text: It is pure water
options.explanation: Pure water sits at pH 7; a value of 11 is far from neutral.

options.text: Its pH says nothing about whether it is an alkali
options.explanation: The pH scale exists precisely to report acidity and alkalinity, and 11 reports alkaline.

check.stem: What is present in every aqueous alkali that makes the solution alkaline?

options.text: Hydroxide ions
options.explanation: The hydroxide ion is what makes an aqueous solution an alkali, whatever the parent base.

options.text: Ammonium ions
options.explanation: Ammonium ions appear only in the ammonia case, not in every alkaline solution.
options.misconception: ammonia case generalised to all alkalis

options.text: Oxide ions
options.explanation: Oxide ions belong to solid metal oxides; in water the hydroxide ion is the marker.

options.text: Hydrogen ions
options.explanation: Hydrogen ions make solutions acidic, the exact opposite of the target.

check.stem: Ammonia solution acts as a base. Why is it described as unusual?

options.text: It is a compound of nitrogen, not a metal oxide or hydroxide
options.explanation: Nearly every base on the course is a metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate, so the nitrogen compound stands out.

options.text: It is the only base that neutralises acids
options.explanation: Every base neutralises acids; that is the family definition, not a special property of ammonia.

options.text: It produces hydrogen ions instead of hydroxide ions in water
options.explanation: Ammonia reacts with water to produce hydroxide ions, which is exactly why it is alkaline.

options.text: It is the only base that dissolves completely in water
options.explanation: Sodium and potassium hydroxide also dissolve freely, so exclusivity is false.

lessons.title: Some common alkalis and the ions they contain
sourceHeadings: Some common alkalis and the ions they contain
lessons.opening: The alkalis met by name at this level are sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and ammonia solution. Each one releases hydroxide ions when it mixes with water, and it is those ions that give the mixture its alkaline behaviour. Ammonia is the odd one out, because the gas itself contains no hydroxide and only produces the ions after reacting with water.
keyPoints: The hydroxide ion is what makes an aqueous solution alkaline.
Sodium hydroxide dissolves in water to give sodium ions and hydroxide ions.
Potassium hydroxide dissolves in water to give potassium ions and hydroxide ions.
Aqueous ammonia contains ammonium ions and hydroxide ions, formed when ammonia reacts with water.
Ammonia is the gas NH3 and ammonium is the ion NH4+, so the two names must not be swapped.

low.restatement: Sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and ammonia solution are the named alkalis, and each supplies hydroxide ions in water. Ammonia gas only makes those ions after it reacts with water, which is why the gas and the solution behave differently.
low.analogy: Ammonia gas joining water to release hydroxide ions is like a dry battery finding its socket: the parts only do their job once they are connected.
low.examPointer: Learn the ion table by heart, and always write ammonia for the gas NH3 and ammonium for the ion NH4+ when naming what you see.

medium.restatement: In water, sodium hydroxide gives Na+ and OH-, potassium hydroxide gives K+ and OH-, and aqueous ammonia gives NH4+ and OH-. The shared OH- ion explains their common alkaline behaviour, while the ammonium ion shows that ammonia reacts with water rather than simply dissolving.
medium.analogy: Three different keys can open the same door when each is cut with the same notch: the shared hydroxide notch is what turns each solution alkaline.
medium.examPointer: Equation questions often want the ammonia-water step made explicit, so state that the gas reacts with water to give ammonium and hydroxide ions.

check.stem: Which ions does aqueous potassium hydroxide contain?

options.text: K+ and OH-
options.explanation: Potassium hydroxide splits into potassium ions and hydroxide ions in water.

options.text: K+ and O2-
options.explanation: The oxide ion belongs to solid oxides; in solution the hydroxide ion carries the alkalinity.

options.text: K2+ and OH-
options.explanation: Potassium is group 1 and forms only 1+ ions, so K2+ is not a real species here.

options.text: K+ and H+
options.explanation: Hydrogen ions would make the solution acidic, not alkaline.

check.stem: Ammonia gas dissolves in water. Which ions appear in the solution?

options.text: NH4+ and OH-
options.explanation: The gas reacts with water to give ammonium ions and hydroxide ions.

options.text: NH3 and OH-
options.explanation: NH3 is the neutral gas molecule, not an ion in the solution.
options.misconception: neutral molecule listed as an ion

options.text: NH4+ and H+
options.explanation: Hydrogen ions would make an acidic solution, but ammonia solution is alkaline.

options.text: N3- and OH-
options.explanation: Nitride ions do not survive in water; the nitrogen appears as ammonium instead.

check.stem: Why must the words ammonia and ammonium not be used interchangeably?

options.text: Ammonia names the gas NH3 while ammonium names the ion NH4+
options.explanation: The gas and the ion are different species, so the names name different things.

options.text: They describe different concentrations of the same solution
options.explanation: The words separate chemical species, not strengths of one solution.

options.text: Ammonium is the unreactive form of ammonia
options.explanation: The ammonium ion takes part in its own chemistry; reactivity is not what separates the words.

options.text: Ammonia is an ion and ammonium is a compound
options.explanation: Both halves of the statement are swapped; ammonia is the gas and ammonium is the ion.

check.stem: A student tests two clear solutions and both turn red litmus paper blue. What can be concluded?

options.text: Both solutions contain hydroxide ions
options.explanation: Alkaline solutions carry hydroxide ions, and that is the only safe shared conclusion.

options.text: Both must be sodium hydroxide
options.explanation: Any alkali turns the paper blue, so the parent base cannot be fixed from this test alone.

options.text: Neither can contain ammonia
options.explanation: Ammonia solution is alkaline and would give exactly this result.

options.text: Both are definitely soluble metal hydroxides
options.explanation: Aqueous ammonia is a counter-example, so the claim is too strong.

check.stem: Which row pairs the alkali with the ions it forms in water?

options.text: Sodium hydroxide gives Na+ and OH-
options.explanation: That is the correct split for sodium hydroxide in water.

options.text: Potassium hydroxide gives K+ and O2-
options.explanation: The hydroxide ion, not the oxide ion, appears when an alkali dissolves.
options.misconception: oxide slip in the ion table

options.text: Aqueous ammonia gives NH3 and OH-
options.explanation: NH3 is the dissolved gas molecule; the ion present is NH4+.
options.misconception: gas molecule listed among the ions

options.text: Sodium hydroxide gives NaOH2- and H+
options.explanation: Neither of those species exists in this solution; sodium and hydroxide ions do.

glossary.definition: A substance that neutralises an acid, forming a salt and water.
A base that is soluble in water.
To cancel out an acid's acidity, producing a salt and water.
The OH- ion, whose presence in water makes the solution alkaline.
The NH4+ ion, formed when ammonia gas reacts with water.

workedExample.prompt: a) State the difference between a base and an alkali, and classify copper(II) oxide. b) Name the ions present in aqueous sodium hydroxide and in aqueous ammonia. c) Why is ammonia gas unusual among bases?
steps: a) A base neutralises an acid to form a salt and water; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Copper(II) oxide is a base but not an alkali, because it is insoluble in water.
b) Sodium hydroxide solution contains Na+ and OH- ions; aqueous ammonia contains NH4+ and OH- ions.
c) The ammonia molecule NH3 contains no hydroxide: it produces OH- ions only after reacting with water, so the gas becomes an alkali only in solution.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Alkalis are soluble bases; CuO is a base only. b) Na+ with OH-; NH4+ with OH-. c) NH3 makes OH- ions only by reacting with water.
